hello.note: Also means 'how are you?'. Hi and hello are just as common; formal: magandang araw po (good day).

goodbye.note: Paalam can sound final. Day to day people say sige po, mauna na po ako (I'll go ahead) or bye.

please.note: Pakiusap is a real plea. For everyday requests add paki- to the verb (pakiabot po = please pass it).

thank_you.note: Very grateful: maraming salamat po. With friends and equals: salamat.

youre_welcome.note: Without po: walang anuman. Casual: wala 'yon (it's nothing) or walang problema.

yes.note: Opo is the respectful yes, for elders and strangers. With friends and equals: oo.

no.note: With friends and equals: hindi. For 'there isn't any / I don't have it' say wala po.

sorry.note: Sorry po is just as common. Formal: paumanhin po.

excuse_me.note: Rather formal. Many simply say excuse me po, or call a stranger ate (to a woman) / kuya (to a man).

how_are_you.note: Kayo is the polite 'you'. With a friend: kumusta ka?

im_fine.note: Casual: okay lang or ayos lang. Ask back with: kayo po? (and you?)

my_name_is.note: Also: ang pangalan ko po ay … . Si is the marker used before a person's name.

nice_to_meet_you.note: Formal. In casual speech many simply say nice to meet you po.

where_from.note: Taga- means 'from (a place)'; the answer uses it too.

im_from.note: Join the place to taga- with a hyphen: taga-Canada po ako.

speak_english.note: Most Filipinos know some English, and mixing both (Taglish) is completely normal.

speak_slowly.note: Shorter and very common: dahan-dahan lang po (slowly, please).

where.note: To ask where something or someone is right now, use nasaan: nasaan po ang …?

what.note: To ask someone to repeat politely: ano po? or just po?

where_bathroom.note: CR (comfort room, said see-ar) is the everyday word for a toilet. Banyo also works.

can_you_help.text: Puwede po ba ninyo akong tulungan?

what_time.note: Clock times use Spanish numbers: alas-dos (two o'clock), alas-singko (five o'clock).

what_means.text: Ano po ang ibig sabihin nito?

one.note: Before a noun it becomes isang: isang tiket (one ticket).

nine.note: In quick speech it often sounds like 'shyam'.

bread.note: Pandesal, the small breakfast roll, is the bread you will see everywhere.

im_hungry.note: Na adds 'already, by now'. To an elder: gutom na po ako.

bill_please.note: In restaurants you will also hear bill out po! or just bill po.

delicious.note: To describe food calmly: masarap po ito (this is tasty).

no_meat.text: Hindi po ako kumakain ng karne
no_meat.note: Karne may be taken as pork and beef only, so also mention manok (chicken) or isda (fish).

enjoy_meal.note: Literally 'let's eat'. Kain tayo! is also a friendly invitation, even to someone passing by.

stop_here.note: On a jeepney or bus, say para po! to get off.

airport.note: Used on signs and in formal Filipino; in everyday speech most people just say airport.

train_station.note: In Metro Manila people usually name the line: istasyon ng MRT / LRT.

want_to_go.note: To a driver, simply: sa … po.

is_it_far.note: On the way: malayo pa po ba? (is it much further?)

one_ticket.note: On jeepneys you pass your fare forward saying bayad po (here's my fare).

too_expensive.note: Naman makes it a gentle complaint. More literal: masyado pong mahal.

cheaper.text: Mayroon po ba kayong mas mura?
cheaper.note: In speech mayroon is usually meron. To haggle: wala na po bang tawad? (no discount?)

id_like_this.note: Literally 'I'll take this'. Pointing and saying ito po (this one) also works.

pay_card.text: Puwede po bang magbayad gamit ang card?
pay_card.note: Also: tumatanggap po ba kayo ng card? (do you take cards?)

cash.note: Filipinos use the English word. Keep barya (coins, small change) for jeepneys and small shops.

open.note: Stress the end: bu-KAS. Said BU-kas it means tomorrow. Many signs are simply in English.

today.note: In speech ngayon (now) alone often means today: ngayon ang alis ko (I leave today).

tomorrow.note: Stress the start: BU-kas. Said bu-KAS it means open. The day after tomorrow: sa makalawa.

later.note: Mamaya means later today. Mamaya na! = not now, later.

good_evening.note: Also said when leaving at night. Good afternoon: magandang hapon po.

good_night.note: Said at bedtime ('sleep soundly'). When leaving at night: magandang gabi po. Many just say good night.

see_you_later.note: Playful and casual: kita-kits! Until next time: hanggang sa muli.

wait_moment.note: Also: saglit lang po. Casual: teka lang (hold on).

help.note: Saklolo! is also understood but sounds old-fashioned.

call_police.note: The emergency number in the Philippines is 911.

dont_feel_well.note: For pain: masakit po ang ulo ko (my head hurts); swap in tiyan (stomach), ngipin (tooth).

pharmacy.note: Drugstore is just as common, especially on signs.

lost_phone.note: Cellphone (or cp, said see-pee) is the everyday word. If stolen: nanakaw po ang cellphone ko.

allergic.note: This is how most people say it. Formal: may alerhiya po ako sa … .

be_careful.note: Ingat! on its own is also a friendly 'take care' when parting.

no_problem.note: With friends: walang problema. Also very common: okay lang po (it's fine).

of_course.note: Often spelled syempre. As a reply to a request: oo naman / opo naman.

maybe.note: Baka also means 'maybe', leaning towards 'it might': baka umulan (it might rain).

dont_know.note: With friends: hindi ko alam. Casual ewan ko can sound curt.

i_like_it.note: In speech ito is often shortened: gusto ko 'to. Gusto also means 'want'.

dont_like_it.note: Blunter and very common: ayoko nito (ayoko = ayaw ko, I don't want).

im_tired.note: To an elder: pagod na po ako.

welcome.note: What hosts say at the door ('come in'). On signs and at events: maligayang pagdating!

congratulations.note: To a friend: binabati kita! Casual and very common: congrats!

mother.note: Formal: ina. Many families say mama or mommy.

father.note: Formal: ama. Many families say papa or daddy.

brother.note: Kapatid alone means sibling. An older brother is called kuya.

sister.note: An older sister is called ate. A younger sibling: nakababatang kapatid.

child.note: Son or daughter: anak na lalaki / anak na babae. A kid in general is bata.

friend.note: Same for men and women. Your close group of friends is your barkada.

this_is_my_friend.note: Same for a male or female friend. With a name: ito po si Ana, kaibigan ko.

are_you_married.text: May asawa na po ba kayo?
are_you_married.note: Literally 'do you have a spouse yet?'. Also: kasal na po ba kayo?

have_children.text: May anak na po ba kayo?
have_children.note: Casual: may anak ka na ba?

monday.note: Day names come from Spanish. On Monday: sa Lunes.

weekend.note: Heard in the news; in everyday speech most people just say weekend: sa weekend.

what_day.note: For the date: anong petsa po ngayon?

next_week.note: This week: ngayong linggo. Last week: noong isang linggo.

eleven.note: Teens are labing- plus the number. For prices many use Spanish (onse) or English.

twelve.note: Labing- shortens before some sounds: labindalawa, labintatlo, labinlima.

fifteen.note: Spanish kinse is just as common for money: kinse pesos.

twenty.note: 21 is dalawampu't isa ('t = at, and). For prices Spanish bente is everyday.

thirty.note: Spanish trenta is everyday for prices and ages: trenta pesos.

fifty.note: Spanish singkwenta is very common: singkwenta pesos.

hundred.note: Also sandaan. 200: dalawang daan. For prices English (one hundred pesos) is very common.

thousand.note: Also sanlibo. 2,000: dalawang libo. 10,000: sampung libo.

years_old.note: The number takes -ng (na after a consonant): dalawampung taon, apat na taon. Casual: bente na ako.

red.note: Before a noun it takes -ng: pulang kotse (red car).

blue.note: Bughaw is the native word, heard mostly in songs and poetry.

green.note: Luntian is the native word, used in formal writing.

black.note: After a consonant the link is na: itim na sapatos (black shoes).

what_colour.note: In a shop, to ask for other colours: may iba pa po bang kulay?

this_one.note: To settle on it: ito na lang po (I'll just take this one).

that_one.note: For something near the person you're talking to, say iyan po. Often shortened: 'yon po, 'yan po.

another_one.note: Nga softens it: isa pa nga po. For a different one: iba naman po.

its_hot.note: A calmer statement: mainit ngayon. Very hot: ang init-init!

its_cold.note: A calmer statement: malamig ngayon. Often said about strong air-con, too.

its_raining.note: Looks like rain: mukhang uulan. Heavy rain: malakas ang ulan.

its_sunny.note: Maaraw ngayon = it's sunny today. Harsh midday sun: tirik na tirik ang araw.

its_windy.note: Strong wind: malakas ang hangin. A storm or typhoon is bagyo.

weather_today.note: Panahon means weather, but also time or season.

beautiful_day.note: Magandang araw is a greeting (good day), not a comment on the weather.

summer.note: Also tag-araw. The Philippines has a hot dry season (tag-init) and a rainy season (tag-ulan).

winter.note: There is no winter in the Philippines; the word is used for colder countries.

have_reservation.note: Many use the English word: may reservation po ako. Under a name: nakapangalan po kay Santos.

passport.note: Passport in English is just as common.

luggage.note: A suitcase is maleta. Your things in general: gamit.

wifi_password.text: Ano po ang password ng Wi-Fi?

check_out_time.note: Check-in and check-out are used just as in English.

bus.note: Same word as in English. Other everyday rides: jeepney (dyip), tricycle and the MRT/LRT trains.

next_train.text: Anong oras po ang susunod na tren?
next_train.note: For any transport: anong oras po ang susunod na biyahe? (next trip)

is_this_seat_free.note: Literally 'is someone sitting here?'. Also: bakante po ba ito? Rito is dito after a vowel.

i_work_in.note: Sa covers places and fields: sa bangko (a bank), sa ospital, sa sales.

im_student.note: Same for men and women. Formal: mag-aaral.

meeting.note: Formal. At work most people simply say meeting (also spelled miting).

im_busy.note: Very common: busy ako. To an elder: abala po ako.

day_off.note: Most people just say day off. No work or school that day: walang pasok.

colleague.note: Same for men and women. Formal: kasamahan sa trabaho.

lets_start.note: Also very common: umpisahan na natin. Natin is 'we' including the listener.

good_job.note: Also very common: ang galing mo! (you're so good), or good job! in English.

table_for_two.note: Staff often ask ilan po kayo? (how many?); just answer dalawa po.

what_recommend.note: Literally 'what's good here?'. Also common: ano po ang best seller ninyo?

not_spicy.note: Also: walang sili po (no chili). Most Filipino dishes are mild anyway.

vegetarian_food.note: Walang karne (no meat) can still mean fish or chicken; say puro gulay (only vegetables).

more_water.note: Pa adds 'more': pahingi pa po ng kanin (more rice, please).

no_sugar.note: Less sugar: kaunting asukal lang po.

im_full.note: To an elder: busog na po ako. Very full: busog na busog na ako.

takeaway.note: This is what everyone says. For leftovers: pakibalot po (please wrap it).

it_was_delicious.note: Adjectives have no tense: masarap = is or was tasty. To the cook: ang sarap po ng luto ninyo!

keep_change.text: Sa inyo na po ang sukli
keep_change.note: Shorter: sa inyo na po. To a friend or someone younger: sa iyo na.

stomach.note: In quick speech it often sounds like 'tyan'.

head_hurts.note: Swap the body part: tiyan (stomach), lalamunan (throat), likod (back).

have_fever.note: A slight fever is sinat: sinisinat po ako.

medicine.note: At a pharmacy: may gamot po ba kayo para sa lagnat? (for a fever)

call_ambulance.note: Kayo addresses everyone around you. Also spelled ambulansiya.

feel_better.text: Mabuti na po ang pakiramdam ko
feel_better.note: Casual: okay na ako. Also: gumaan na po ang pakiramdam ko (I feel lighter).

get_well.note: Sana = I hope. To a friend: sana gumaling ka agad! Short and casual: pagaling ka!

lets_meet.note: Casual: kita tayo! Add a day: magkita tayo sa Sabado.

are_you_free.note: Casual: libre ka ba bukas? Also: may gagawin ka ba bukas? (any plans?)

call_me.note: Casual: tawagan mo ako. Text me: i-text mo ako.

your_number.note: Most people say number and mean the cellphone. Casual: anong number mo?

see_you_soon.note: Playful: kita-kits! Slightly formal: hanggang sa muli (until next time).

have_nice_day.note: When parting, many Filipinos simply say ingat po! (take care).

good_luck.note: Literally 'do it well!'. To wish luck itself: sana suwertehin ka. Good luck! in English is common too.

happy_birthday.note: In speech, happy birthday! is far more common. The birthday song is Maligayang Bati.

miss_you.note: This is how most people say it. Also: nami-miss kita. Deep longing: nangungulila ako sa iyo.
